title: Job's Defense and Divine Providence
english: … him. But who, when he judges, will answer him back?

“Therefore I am dismayed before his face; I will consider, and I shall be terrified of him” (Job 23:15). I have not sinned, he says, and what of that? For God is free to punish not only by the right that sins give him; this too, I say, he may do without any sins.

“For I did not know that darkness would come upon me, and before my face thick gloom covered me” (Job 23:17). This did not happen in the ordinary human course of things, he says: the evil was unforeseen, and I judge the blow to be from the hand of God. And he rightly said “before my face,” for the darkness is not shared by all; it belongs to my own despondency.

“But why has he himself made no visitation of these? They were on the earth, and they did not recognise it” (Job 24:12-13). That is: they despised everyone, they laughed at everyone; no one wrongs them or does them harm. But he has not yet made a visitation of them, so he will do it afterwards: he will examine the offences they have committed and will not overlook them. Greedily they devoured orphans.
“And knowing their works, he handed them over to darkness” (Job 24:14). That is, having learned their works; or else, having examined them and put them to the test: that is what “knowing” means.

“Nor will my soul meditate unjust things” (Job 27:4). That is: I will stand by the same verdict. No one will be able to turn me aside, no one to break in on me, no one to lead me away from what lies before me.

“Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die, for I will not put away my innocence” (Job 27:5). That is: I will not accuse myself, nor change my ground, even if you say ten thousand things; I will not give up my verdict, even if you seem to have dropped your charge against me. Should I assent to what you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would be declaring you righteous. I will not thrust away my innocence by thinking one thing about you and saying another.

“Or when distress comes upon him, has he any boldness before him?” (Job 27:9-10). What he says amounts to this: the one who does wrong, he says, has no boldness, neither to utter a sound nor to say the things that I am saying now; it has been taken from him and he has been muzzled. But this has not happened to me: I speak, and I answer back. The unjust are not so.
“For there is a place for silver,” and so on (Job 28:1). He says this: the one who fixed an order in ordinary things has done so far more in human affairs.

“For iron comes from the earth, and bronze is quarried like stone. He has set an order for darkness, and he himself searches out every limit” (Job 28:2-3). That is, he exercises providence and cares for affairs, and nothing passes by idly or at random. Or rather, he is saying this: other things are plain, but God's dispensation cannot be traced and is unknown. And a little after: He said well, “He has set an order for darkness,” showing that it knows how to give way and to withdraw altogether. Who drives away that gloom? Where does such good order come from in such a thing? Then he recounts his power, and then his wisdom, persuading one not to wish to call him to account.

“As when his lamp shone above my head, when by his light I walked in darkness” (Job 29:3). That he sought his former prosperity for this reason, so that God's providence might be shown, is clear from his saying, “When God guarded me” (Job 29:2).

“When God watched over my house” (Job 29:4). Symmachus: “When God fenced round my tent.” You see that this is what he longed for: to show God's oversight and providence. When I was young and had means, being righteous, he says, I made the material that served me into virtue, for I used everything well.

“When I went out early into the city, and my seat was set in the squares” (Job 29:7). For like a ruler and teacher of virtue, he did not give his time to sleep and drinking, but out of love sat at daybreak in the squares, becoming a law and a pattern to those in the city.
“May the blessing of one who was perishing come upon me” (Job 29:13).
From Severus, from the letter to Juliana the deaconess: The Lord says in the Gospels, about those who make themselves dead to the world …

added_allusions.note: Possible echo only: 'who, when he judges, will answer him back?' recalls LXX 23:13 τίς ὁ ἀντερῶν αὐτῷ; it is the commentator's phrase, not a lemma, and KJV 23:13 ('who can turn him?') differs, so not cited in the text.
